thread.title: Kia Niro May Be The Next Budget EV Sales Success In Europe - Hyundai Motor Co., Ltd. (OTCMKTS:HYMLF)

author: Anton Wahlman
title: Kia Niro May Be The Next Budget EV Sales Success In Europe - Hyundai Motor Co., Ltd. (OTCMKTS:HYMLF)
text:
Late in the day on November 21, Tesla's (NASDAQ: TSLA ) Elon Musk tweeted that he was “signing off for a while”: here. By any normal definition, that doesn’t mean “Going to bed, and enjoying Thanksgiving Day.”
Rather, one would presume that it meant something more significant than barely the overnight body clock and a turkey meal. “Signing off” would be more like Elvis Presley ceasing live concerts for eight years in the 1960s. Well, in Elon’s case that didn’t last anywhere near that long. By the time the market closed on Friday November 23, Elon was at it again with an important message: here.
In what seems like the oddest of moves, Elon tweeted out a highly outdated article from January 7, which lists the EVs on sale in the U.S. at that time. Considering how frequently new EVs are coming onto the market right now, it was about as relevant as tweeting out the “news” that the Apple ( AAPL ) iPhone 7 had made it to market.
That list from January 7 simply has no relevancy in terms of what is happening in the EV market right now. Most importantly, the Jaguar i-Pace wasn’t on that list, which already started U.S. deliveries, and neither was the Audi eTron, for which you can place a $1,000 deposit as of September 17, 2018, and take delivery in the U.S. the second quarter of 2019. Furthermore, the Hyundai Kona EV deliveries are starting in the U.S. in December 2018 - a couple of weeks from now.
Then again, the U.S. isn’t the frontier for EV competition anyway. By at least some sort of definition, China is the ultimate frontier for EV competition. Just look at the October 2018 sales chart: here. Most people could not identify a single name on that top-20 list.
Considering that Tesla isn’t a meaningful competitive factor in China, and that not a single one of the top-20 best-selling EVs on that list will ever be sold in the U.S. and probably not in Europe either, it doesn’t have much relevance to the U.S. or to Tesla. But you know what does have relevance to the U.S. and to Tesla? Europe.
The cars that are and will be available in the U.S. and Europe are and will largely be the same. Not 100% of them, but most of the best sellers are or will soon be. Some obviously sell more here vs there. By and large, all other things equal, Europeans prefer cars made in Europe (Nissan ( OTCPK:NSANY ) LEAF, BMW i3, Renault Zoe and Volkswagen eGolf), whereas Americans award higher market shares to U.S.-manufactured models (Tesla and Chevrolet).
Where Europe does differ from the U.S. is that there are some jurisdictions in Europe that have larger EV adoption than the U.S. Norway is the standout example, of course, as its 50%-plus plug-in adoption puts it close to a full decimal point ahead of most other countries, even in Europe, let alone the U.S. For this reason, some automakers tend to make the most EV-friendly European jurisdictions into the competitive frontier for new models when they first make it out of the factory.
That’s why Elon Musk’s swift return from Thanksgiving hiatus tweet about a competitive list regarding the U.S. dated January 7 was doubly irrelevant. It was an hopelessly old document, and it did not concern the frontier of the EV competitive landscape, which is Europe in general, and Norway in particular.

However, there's more to the emerging EV competition story than just those sales numbers. Analysts also have to consider what is coming right around the corner - cars that you can order, but are being delivered in the next few weeks and months.
So let’s take a look at what Elon ought to have examined instead, and what the new emerging star on the EV competitive horizon may be, as the European EV calendar turns from December 31 to January 1.
Late 2018 has seen new electric car successes in Europe come on hard and fast. It started already in March 2018 with the 151-mile range version of the Nissan LEAF, which now comfortably leads the European sales charts. As you can see in the table above, Nissan sold 34,180 LEAFs in Europe through October. That puts it easily as the No. 1 electric car seller in Europe: here. Only the alliance-partner Renault, with the Zoe, comes even remotely close in the European rankings.
Then, in September 2018, Hyundai started European deliveries of the Kona EV and Jaguar with the i-Pace. Hyundai ( OTCPK:HYMLF ) has been very supply-constrained, although that is supposed to change “soon,” whatever that means: here. I drove the Hyundai Kona EV on U.S. soil in the first half of October, and will be publishing my review soon - hopefully shortly after Hyundai announces its U.S. price of this product. It's scheduled to go on sale in the U.S. in December 2018.
In any case, as of this writing (Sunday evening, Norway time), Hyundai had sold 625 Kona EV units in Norway since it started two months ago. As I showed in the table above, In November to date, that puts the Kona EV sales at almost exactly the same levels as Tesla Model S: 109 units for each car.
As you can see in the table above, the Kona EV isn’t even the best-selling Hyundai BEV in Norway. That’s the Ioniq EV, which is not an SUV and which has about half the range of the Kona EV. That tells you that the Kona EV is supply constrained more than anything - it ought to be selling a lot more than the Ioniq EV.
Somewhere half way between the Hyundai Kona EV and the Ioniq EV, in terms of Norwegian sales, we find the Kia ( OTCPK:KIMTF ) Soul EV. This car has been around longer than the Ioniq EV and doesn’t get as good a range either. But it speaks to the public’s love for the square and tall body shape, which the Soul possesses aplenty. More about that below, as an all-new Kia Soul EV arrives in just a few short months from now.
Next on deck for European BEV sales will be the Audi eTron : here. It entered production in early September, and Audi’s head of the Brussels factory where the car is made said at the Sept. 17 introduction that the production capacity is 200 cars per day. It was unclear whether they were actually producing at that rate already, or if that was a rate to be achieved in the coming months.
The Audi eTron is ever so slightly larger and more expensive than the Jaguar i-Pace, and unless there are any further delays, it will begin deliveries in The Netherlands and a few other European countries such as Belgium, Germany and Norway, around the end of December - barely a few weeks from now.
However, within days or weeks of the Audi eTron’s appearance in European showrooms, a car that's expected to be barely half the price of the Audi eTron also will become available there: The Kia Niro EV. Unlike other Kia-Hyundai “sister” products, it’s far from clear whether the Kia Niro EV will simply be a Hyundai Kona EV with a different body. It’s possible that, for example, the battery used - while of a similar nominal capacity - will be composed by completely different battery cells. We will know those technical details very soon.
The first boats from Korea with the Kia Niro EV arrive in Europe in December, and official sales of the Kia Niro EV are scheduled to start in some countries in Europe on January 1. It looks to me a like a very coordinated and deliberate launch.
There are good reasons why the Kia Niro may do even better than the other Kia-Hyundai BEV products in Europe:
Kia Soul EV
Hyundai Ioniq EV
Hyundai Kona EV
Why?
Kia Soul EV: It has a lot less range than any of the other products. Despite this, it has sold 5,266 units in Europe for the first three quarters of 2018.
Hyundai Ioniq EV: It's a lower car, as far from a crossover-SUV as it comes, and it has approximately half the range of the upcoming Kia Niro EV. Yet, it sold 6,610 units in Europe through the first three quarters of 2018.
Hyundai Kona EV: This car checks all the boxes - long range and SUV body/looks. However, it has been gravely supply constrained. If the Kia Niro EV gets around that kind of constraint, it could pick up huge sales.
Then we have the pink elephant in the middle of the room: Tesla Model 3. It's supposed to arrive in Europe in late February or March, following the January production start in the only factory in which it is made: Fremont, CA. However, Tesla has not yet announced that it has been approved for sale in Europe.
I assume that it will be approved for sale in Europe, in time for deliveries to take place by March. However, there's a non-zero risk factor for Tesla here. For those of us not privy to Tesla’s interactions with the European regulators and other authorities, we simply cannot know the status of this approval process. Is it happening or is it not? Are there issues Tesla first has to solve/change? If so, how long will that realistically take?
Therefore, not knowing with 100% certainty whether or when the Tesla Model 3 will be approved for European consumption, we know at least one thing for sure: The Kia Niro EV will be making its first deliveries in Europe in early January 2019. The range will be similar to the base Tesla Model 3. It will have a taller and more square-ish body style, which is what most people in Europe want, along with that hatchback-wagon profile Kia has perfected with the Niro and Soul.
If Kia can only prevent the kind of supply constraints that bedeviled the Hyundai Kona EV for its first few months of European market introduction, the Kia Niro EV looks to become the “new hot EV” in the European market starting early January 2019. I know this may be a bit difficult to understand for U.S.-based Tesla fans, but it may prove to be the most desirable “budget” EV in the European market for the first part of 2019 - attempting to challenge the market share leaders from Nissan, Renault, Volkswagen and BMW.
I could stop right here, but there's an additional twist to this story that warrants mention. While the Kia Niro EV will have approximately 260 miles of range on the U.S. EPA cycle (higher on the European test cycle), it will not be Kia’s only new EV in 2019. By the late spring 2019, Kia also will have the all-new version of the Kia Soul EV in dealerships: here.
So what’s the difference between the Kia Niro EV and the Kia Soul EV? Both have somewhat square and tall body styles, but the Niro will have that longer range of 260 miles. The next-gen Soul will have an EV range of approximately 140-160 miles, thanks to a battery that would be 39-40 kWh. In other words, similar to the current Nissan LEAF, which has a range of 151 miles.
What does that mean, and why is it important? Kia will be able to attack the market at a wide range of price points - from the least expensive with only approximately 150 miles of range, up to Tesla Model 3 class at 260 miles of range. And it will be able to do so with two slightly different - but both most popular body styles, especially in Europe where people prefer hatchbacks and stations wagons over sedans (and the Tesla Model 3 is a sedan, not a hatchback).
Conclusion: The silent EV conglomerate from Korea Kia and Hyundai tend to not get as much attention as most of the other EV players such as General Motors ( GM ) and The Volkswagen Group (including Audi and Porsche) - let alone Tesla. However, when you look at the trajectory in the European (including Norway in particular) EV sales charts over the last couple of months, and then consider what will be in European dealerships in the month of January 2019, you may very well conclude that Kia-Hyundai will be fighting for leadership position in the earliest part of 2019.
It's a very different picture than in China and North America indeed.
